Family Zoo — a Chord tutorial

Sixteen steps through the Sharpee engine

→ Play the finished zoo Play in IF Hub

Family Zoo is a tutorial for Chord, the authoring language of the Sharpee interactive fiction engine. It builds one game across sixteen steps: v01 is a single room in about fifty lines, v16 is the whole zoo in eight hundred — animals with their own verbs, a zookeeper, timed events, scoring, and an after-hours phase.

Every step is a single .story file that is the step before it plus one idea, and every step is playable on its own with its source and test report beside it. Start at v01 to follow it in order, or jump in anywhere.

Current

The finished zoo: eight rooms, animals with their own verbs, a zookeeper, timed events, scoring, and an after-hours phase where the parrot stops being polite. This is every step above, in one 800-line Chord file.

  • `on every turn` — the daemon
  • `define sequence feeding time` — scripted beats in order
  • Gating a daemon on a condition so it is not always talking
  • Keeping ambient text from drowning the player's own actions
  • `use scoring` in the story header
  • `score visit worth 5` on a room

v16 — After Hours & the TypeScript Hatch

The zoo closes. A story state flips, the zookeeper leaves, and the parrot starts speaking candidly — and the parrot's flavour line comes from TypeScript, the one escape hatch Chord keeps.

  • `states: open, after-hours` in the header
  • `while after-hours` on clauses and descriptions
  • `define sequence closing time` driving the transition
  • `define text flavor from "./chord-extras.ts"` (ADR-259)
  • When to reach for the hatch — and when not to

v15 — Scoring & Endgame

Points for seeing the zoo. `use scoring` turns on the SCORE command, rooms carry what a visit is worth, and `award` banks it once.

  • `use scoring` in the story header
  • `score visit worth 5` on a room
  • `award visit` inside `after the player entering`
  • Why awarding is idempotent — revisiting pays nothing
  • The SCORE command, for free

v14 — Daemons & Sequences

The zoo starts moving on its own: PA announcements, feeding time, goats that get hungrier. A daemon runs every turn; a sequence is a scripted run of beats.

  • `on every turn` — the daemon
  • `define sequence feeding time` — scripted beats in order
  • Gating a daemon on a condition so it is not always talking
  • Keeping ambient text from drowning the player's own actions

v13 — Custom Traits & Actions

Goats, rabbits and the verbs that go with them. In Chord a trait and the action that dispatches on it are one lesson: the trait names a capability, the action is what makes it mean something.

  • `define trait pettable` — naming a capability the stdlib lacks
  • `define action petting` — a new verb and its grammar
  • An action that finds its target by trait, not by name
  • `feedable`, `chatty`, `restless` and animals that carry several traits
  • Why a trait alone does nothing until an action consults it

v12 — Event Clauses

The snake, and the three places a story can interrupt the engine: before an action, after it, and on it. This is Chord's answer to event handlers.

  • `on the player ing` — replace the standard response
  • `before` — refuse or redirect an action
  • `after the player entering` — react to arrival
  • Where a clause belongs: on the thing, not in a central handler

v11 — Characters

Sam the zookeeper. A person is created like anything else, but carries conversation and reacts to the player being in the room.

  • `a person` and where they stand
  • `on the player talking to` for conversation
  • Describing someone doing something, not just standing there
  • Why the room description mentions them separately

v10 — Switchable Devices

A radio in the supply room, a feed dispenser in the petting zoo, a penny press in the gift shop — and the shop itself, whose description is stitched from a cycling phrase.

  • `switchable` and TURN ON / TURN OFF
  • `on` clauses that fire when a device is used
  • `define phrase pins, cycling` — a different line each time
  • `{pins}` — binding a phrase into a description

v09 — Readable Objects

A plaque in the aviary. READ is its own action, distinct from EXAMINE, and a phrase block lets the text be laid out the way a sign really reads.

  • `readable` alongside `scenery`
  • `on the player reading` versus the plain description
  • A `phrase` block holding multi-paragraph sign text
  • Why READ and EXAMINE should say different things

v08 — Light & Dark

The nocturnal exhibit is unlit. Without a light source the player sees nothing; with the flashlight the room opens up. One word on the room does the whole job.

  • `a room, dark`
  • A portable light source and what carrying it changes
  • What the engine says when there is no light
  • A warning sign that tells the player what they need

v07 — Locked Doors & Keys

A staff gate the player cannot pass until they find the keycard. The refusal message is a named phrase in the en-US catalog, not hardcoded English in the exit.

  • `lockable with the staff keycard`
  • `south is blocked while the staff gate is closed: staff-gate-blocked`
  • `define phrases en-US` — the catalog of refusal keys
  • UNLOCK, LOCK and the messages the stdlib already knows

v06 — Openable Things

The supply room, its metal shelves and a cork board. `openable` gives a thing an open and a closed state, and OPEN and CLOSE start working with no code of your own.

  • `openable` and the state it implies
  • A container that is also openable
  • Rooms reached only through something you must open
  • Descriptions that read correctly whether open or closed

v05 — Containers & Supporters

A backpack that holds things and a park bench that things sit on. Chord distinguishes what is *in* a thing from what is *on* it, and the parser follows.

  • `a container` — things go in it
  • `a supporter` — things go on it
  • Putting a thing inside another at creation time
  • How the room description reports contents it did not have to be told about

v04 — Portable Objects

The first things the player can carry: a brochure, a map, a souvenir penny. Also the first phrase block — the brochure's text is set verbatim so its layout survives.

  • A thing with no `scenery` is takeable by default
  • `readable` and `on the player reading`
  • `define phrase brochure-text, verbatim` — text kept exactly as written
  • TAKE, DROP and INVENTORY come from the standard library

v03 — Scenery

Fences, flower beds, hay, a waterfall, a toucan. Scenery is what makes a room feel like a place rather than a list of exits — present to examine, refused when taken.

  • `scenery` blocks taking without any refusal message of your own
  • Several scenery things sharing one room
  • Writing descriptions that reward a second look
  • `aka` on scenery so EXAMINE FENCE and EXAMINE IRON FENCE both work

v02 — Multiple Rooms & Navigation

The zoo grows to four rooms joined by compass directions. Exits are one line each, and `aka` gives every room the names a player will actually type.

  • `south to the Main Path` — an exit is a property of the room
  • Exits are declared one way; Chord wires the return trip
  • `aka path, gravel path` for synonyms the parser accepts
  • Room descriptions that tell the player where the exits go

v01 — A Single Room

The smallest Chord story that runs: a header that names the work, one room, and two pieces of scenery you can examine. Everything else in the tutorial is added to this.

  • The `story` header — `title`, `authors`, `id`, `description`
  • `create the ` with `a room` and an indented description
  • `scenery` for things that belong to the room and cannot be taken
  • `in the ` to place a thing
  • `before the game starts` naming who the player is
